questions.explanation: A forward CG increases the nose-down moment, requiring a greater tail-down force to balance. This effectively increases the wing loading and raises the stalling speed. However, it also increases the stabilising moment arm, improving longitudinal stability and control authority.

questions.question: An aft CG position will result in:-

options.text: a lower stalling speed but reduced longitudinal stability
a higher stalling speed and greater stability

questions.explanation: An aft CG reduces the tail-down force needed to balance the aircraft, effectively reducing wing loading and lowering the stalling speed. However, the reduced moment arm between CG and tailplane decreases longitudinal stability, making the aircraft harder to control in pitch.

questions.question: The purpose of the horizontal stabiliser (tailplane) is to provide:-
questions.explanation: The horizontal stabiliser provides longitudinal (pitch) stability. In most aircraft, it produces a downward force to balance the nose-heavy moment created by the CG being forward of the CP. If the aircraft is disturbed in pitch, the tailplane generates a restoring moment.

questions.question: The purpose of the vertical stabiliser (fin) is to provide:-
questions.explanation: The vertical stabiliser (fin) provides directional (yaw) stability about the normal axis. If the aircraft yaws, the fin presents an angle of attack to the relative airflow, generating a side force that weathercocks the aircraft back to its original heading.

questions.question: A phugoid oscillation is a long-period oscillation involving:-

options.text: changes in pitch attitude, altitude, and airspeed at approximately constant angle of attack
rapid changes in angle of attack at constant speed
rapid pitch oscillations at constant altitude

questions.explanation: A phugoid is a long-period longitudinal oscillation where the aircraft exchanges kinetic and potential energy. The nose pitches up (speed decreases, altitude increases), then pitches down (speed increases, altitude decreases). The AoA remains approximately constant. In a stable aircraft, the oscillation damps out over time.

questions.question: Dutch roll is an oscillation that involves:-

options.text: a combination of yaw and roll

questions.explanation: Dutch roll is a coupled lateral-directional oscillation involving simultaneous yawing and rolling motions. It occurs when the aircraft has more lateral stability than directional stability. The nose traces a figure-eight pattern. It can be uncomfortable for passengers and is suppressed by yaw dampers in larger aircraft.

questions.question: Spiral instability occurs when an aircraft has:-

options.text: more directional stability than lateral stability
more lateral stability than directional stability
positive static stability in all axes

questions.explanation: Spiral instability occurs when directional stability is strong relative to lateral stability. If the aircraft is disturbed in roll, the yaw due to sideslip (strong directional stability) increases the bank angle faster than the dihedral effect (weak lateral stability) can correct it, leading to an ever-tightening spiral dive.

questions.question: The total drag on an aircraft is the sum of:-

options.text: form drag and skin friction drag only
induced drag and form drag only
skin friction drag and interference drag only

questions.explanation: Total drag = induced drag + parasite drag. Induced drag is the drag associated with lift production (wingtip vortices). Parasite drag is all other drag (form drag + skin friction + interference drag) not related to lift production.

questions.question: At speeds below the minimum drag speed (on the back side of the drag curve), if the pilot reduces speed further:-

options.text: total drag increases and more power is required to maintain level flight
parasite drag increases more than induced drag

questions.explanation: Below the minimum drag speed, the aircraft is in the 'region of reversed command' or 'back side of the drag curve'. Reducing speed further increases induced drag (due to higher AoA) more than parasite drag decreases. Total drag increases, requiring more power to maintain level flight. This is an unstable speed regime.

questions.question: The region of reversed command refers to the speed range where:-

options.text: a decrease in speed requires an increase in power to maintain altitude
an increase in speed requires an increase in power

questions.explanation: In the region of reversed command (below minimum drag speed), the normal relationship between speed and power is reversed. Normally, slowing down requires less power. But in this region, slowing down increases induced drag so much that MORE power is needed. This is critical during slow-speed operations like approach and landing.

questions.question: The effect of increasing altitude on TAS, for a given IAS, is that TAS will:-
questions.explanation: IAS reflects dynamic pressure (½ρV²). At higher altitude, air density (ρ) is lower. To produce the same dynamic pressure (same IAS reading), the actual velocity (TAS) must be higher. As a rule of thumb, TAS increases by approximately 2% per 1000 ft above sea level.

questions.question: Indicated airspeed (IAS) is:-

options.text: the airspeed shown on the airspeed indicator, uncorrected for errors
the true speed of the aircraft through the air
the speed of the aircraft over the ground

questions.explanation: IAS is the reading on the airspeed indicator (ASI) before any corrections. It contains instrument error and position error. CAS is IAS corrected for these errors. TAS is CAS corrected for non-standard density (temperature and pressure). Groundspeed is TAS corrected for wind.

questions.question: Calibrated airspeed (CAS) is:-

options.text: IAS corrected for instrument and position errors
the speed shown on the ASI

questions.explanation: CAS is obtained by correcting IAS for instrument error (inaccuracies in the ASI mechanism) and position error (caused by the location of the pitot tube and static ports on the aircraft). CAS is then corrected for density to obtain TAS.

questions.question: A propeller blade is twisted from root to tip so that:-

options.text: the angle of attack remains approximately constant along the blade
the blade is stronger at the root
the blade produces more thrust at the tip
the blade is easier to manufacture

questions.explanation: The tip of a propeller blade moves faster than the root (greater circumference). Without twist, the tip would have a much lower angle of attack than the root. The blade is twisted so the pitch angle decreases from root to tip, maintaining a roughly constant AoA along the entire blade for efficient thrust production.

questions.question: The blade angle of a propeller is the angle between:-

options.text: the chord line of the blade and the plane of rotation
the chord line and the relative airflow
the blade and the longitudinal axis of the aircraft
the leading edge and the trailing edge

questions.explanation: The blade angle (pitch angle) is the angle between the chord line of the propeller blade section and the plane of rotation (perpendicular to the propeller shaft). It is a geometric angle set by design (fixed-pitch) or adjustable (variable-pitch). It is not the same as the blade's angle of attack.

questions.question: As forward speed increases with a fixed-pitch propeller, the angle of attack of the propeller blade:-
questions.explanation: The propeller blade's AoA is the difference between the blade angle and the helix angle (determined by the ratio of forward speed to rotational speed). As forward speed increases, the helix angle increases, reducing the blade's effective AoA. This is why a fixed-pitch propeller loses efficiency at speeds far from its design speed.

questions.question: A leading edge slot on a wing is designed to:-

options.text: delay the stall by energising the boundary layer at high angles of attack
reduce parasite drag at cruise speed
increase the maximum speed of the aircraft

questions.explanation: A leading edge slot is a gap between the leading edge slat and the main wing. At high AoA, high-pressure air from below flows through the slot over the upper surface, energising the boundary layer and delaying separation. This increases the critical AoA and reduces the stalling speed.

questions.question: Vortex generators are small fins mounted on the wing surface to:-

options.text: energise the boundary layer and delay flow separation

questions.explanation: Vortex generators are small vertical fins that create small vortices in the boundary layer. These vortices mix high-energy air from outside the boundary layer with the slower air near the surface, energising it and delaying separation. This improves control effectiveness and can reduce stalling speed.

questions.question: The effect of extending the landing gear (undercarriage) in flight is to:-
questions.explanation: Extending the landing gear exposes additional structure to the airflow, significantly increasing form drag (a component of parasite drag). This is why retractable gear aircraft have better cruise performance — the gear is stowed to reduce drag. Some pilots use gear extension as a speed brake.

questions.question: The critical angle of attack for a typical light aircraft aerofoil is approximately:-
questions.explanation: The critical (stalling) angle of attack for most conventional aerofoils used on light aircraft is approximately 15-17° (commonly stated as about 16°). Beyond this angle, the airflow separates from the upper surface and lift decreases dramatically. This angle is constant regardless of speed, weight, or altitude.

questions.question: The three axes of an aircraft all pass through the:-
questions.explanation: All three axes of flight — lateral (pitch), longitudinal (roll), and normal/vertical (yaw) — intersect at the centre of gravity. The CG is the point about which all rotations occur. This is why CG position is so critical to aircraft stability and control.
